subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
As I listened this afternoon to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) I was amazed to hear him say that he was opposed to conscription and that no political party with any regard for their political future would ever think of putting conscription in force in this country. I am amazed that a member of the cabinet at this
3340	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (Souris)
time should think for a moment of party before country. Apparently the hon. gentleman is still travelling in the middle of the road as he was in March, 1940. Surely we should endeavour to save the country in manly fashion for our children and for the generations to come, whether as individuals we ever come back to parliament or not, because we should realize that should we lose the war this nation will be disgraced for many generations to come.
The bill before us follows in consequence of the plebiscite. This plebiscite was the strangest and most cumbersome manoeuvre ever conceived and imposed upon the people in the name of national unity, by any country. It has given needless emphasis to a division in the country's make-up which everyone knew beforehand existed, a division that exists chiefly as a result of the attitude and example of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the first great world war from 1914 to 1918, and in his leadership and appeal during the past twenty-five years in this country-all for political expediency. This is well borne out in the speech on foreign policy which he delivered in this chamber on March 30, 1939, as reported at page 2426 of Hansard:
One strategic fact is clear: the days of great expeditionary forces of infantry crossing the oceans are not likely to recur Two years ago, I expressed in this house the view that it was extremely doubtful if any of the British dominions would ever send another expeditionary force to Europe.
One political fact is equally clear: in a war to save the liberty of others, and thus our own, we should not sacrifice our own liberty or our own unity. Planning and coordination would be essential, but the necessary coordination could be made, and if this government were in power it would be made, without sacrificing those vital ends and conditions of our existence. Profits could and would be rigidly controlled, and profiteering suppressed. But men's lives and men's wills cannot be put on the same basis as goods and profits. The present government believes that conscription of men for overseas service would not be a necessary or an effective step. Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
That is not so different from the speech which the Minister of Agriculture quoted this afternoon concerning the member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell)-very similar in fact. I vigorously opposed the plebiscite as being the negation of parliamentary responsibility; but when the government carried the measure I submitted to majority rule in the house and went out to assist in every way possible to obtain an affirmative vote, and I was pleased to see that Canada voted two to one "yes" on the plebiscite. It is said that the plebiscite was not a vote either for or against

compulsory overseas service. No; nothing as straightforward as that was meant by that vote. On June 11, I listened to that great speech delivered by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). He maintained that when the people of Quebec voted "no" they voted against conscription for overseas service, but he did not think many of those who voted "yes" voted for conscription. Surely by the same token, if those people who voted "no" voted against conscription for overseas service, those who voted "yes," the vast majority, voted for conscription for overseas service. What did the Prime Minister mean in his broadcast on April 7, after pointing out the dangerous situation that existed in Canada, both east and west, and in Europe, when he spoke as follows:
We cannot defend our country and save our homes and families by waiting at home for the enemy to attack us. Every country that has stood behind its own defences in this war has sooner or later been attacked. To remain on the defensive is the surest way to bring the war to Canada. We must go out and meet the enemy before he reaches our shores. If you cannot trust parliament, your own elected representatives, whom can you trust!
On the basis of those words I think we should be entitled to discuss this bill in a mandatory form before this house. The logical conclusion for the people of Canada to arrive at was that if they released the Prime Minister from his pledge, then soldiers would be sent to any theatre of war, as is done by our good neighbour and ally, the United States of America, and we would no longer be looked upon by them as a nation in disgrace, as we are at this time. Here in the House of Commons is the place and now is the time to discuss and determine whether and by what methods the resources and man-power of this nation shall be mobilized. Parliament and not the cabinet in secrecy is the proper body to discuss these measures. I remember reading earnestly the debates during the year 1932, I having lived in the drought area of the west at that time. I wonder to-day if the Prime Minister is the same man who led the opposition during those debates and protested so vigorously over the fact that Prime Minister Bennett should be given a blank cheque to feed and clothe those people who were suffering as a result of the drought, and who were on relief, throughout the greater part of that section. He protested severely, and yet in this debate he asks the people for a blank cheque which enables him, if the occasion arises, to dispose of those same lives that were then being cared for. There is not much consistency in that stand. If the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres

Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (Souris)
thinks that the Prime Minister has betrayed the people of Quebec, then in my opinion there are many people in eight other provinces who also feel that the Prime Minister has betrayed them to some extent.
I presume that during this debate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will speak and endeavour to prove how satisfactorily the voluntary system is working to-day. During the campaign in 1917 for a national government in this country, Major J. L. Ralston, then serving in France, wrote letters to the Halifax papers urging the people to support a national government in Canada at that time. Speaking at Charlottetown during the plebiscite campaign this year, in appealing for a "yes" vote, he said, "We must back up our boys overseas." Speaking in Winnipeg on May 25, 1942, before the Canadian Legion convention, Colonel Ralston promised a relentless war effort. He spoke of our man-power problems, stating that competition and wages had attracted men from one job to another. He said that this had, in many instances, left useful jobs with too few men to do them. Key men from industry and agriculture had, he said, joined the armed forces in many instances. Notwithstanding the splendid speech delivered that day by our senior Minister of National Defence on the achievements of our armed forces and on industrial expansion to date in Canada, the following day that great non-political organization representing the nine provinces of Canada passed a unanimous resolution for total war and asked for immediate conscription for overseas service. I contend that no organization in Canada has done more to assist the government in the war effort than the Canadian Legion.
I have the privilege and honour of representing a constituency that polled the greatest percentage of "yes" over "no" votes of any rural riding in Canada, the proportion being over sixteen to one. The only riding in Canada to surpass that record was Eglinton in the city of Toronto. The constituency of Souris is predominantly Anglo-Saxon, but there is one solid French polling division in it, and they voted "yes" in the proportion of well over two to one. There is a predominantly Mennonite polling division; they voted "yes", 128 to "no" 12. My home town of Melita polled 531 "yes" and 8 "no". Of two small rural school divisions, Bede voted 71 "yes", none "no"; and Swaffan, 56 "yes", and none "no". Fifty-four polling divisions in the constituency voted 8.043 "yes", and 484	"no". The municipal officials, legion
officials, church and other community organizations, along with the general public, 44561-212
demonstrated a keen sense of citizenship and of public duty in so doing. At every meeting which I addressed in the riding during that plebiscite campaign I referred to my plea to the government on November 10, 1941, in this house for immediate national selective service in any theatre of war. At the same time I told them that the Prime Minister had said that they were not voting for or against conscription and that I had no idea what they might get as a result. While the people considered the plebiscite useless they now expect some immediate action.
The province of Manitoba voted "yes" almost five to one despite the isolationist and non-conscription views of our two federal cabinet ministers.
The press of Canada on June 3, 1942, quoting the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler), which constituency adjoins mine on the east, said that he had stated:
Many old heads in Ottawa say when the government falls, as all things eventually must, it will not be over conscription. ...
The advice of the government's wartime specialists is going to govern. There is no escaping it. The government only has all the facts, they and only they. Theirs is the responsibility and theirs the decision.
But the opposition is lying awake nights thinking of formulae which by way of amendment they can embarrass supporters in the eyes of their constituents.
The Tories will try to embarrass government supporters before their "yes" (plebiscite) voters.
There is no one in the opposition who could do that job half as well as it has been done by those hon. members themselves. In the constituency of Lisgar during the plebiscite there was an available vote of 14,658. There was a "yes" vote of 4,633 and a "no" vote of 620. Poll No. 32, Rhineland, with 249 available votes, polled no votes either "yes" or "no". Poll No. 32A Rhineland, with 220 available votes, polled no votes "yes" or "no". Poll No. 21A, Winkler, with 287 available votes, polled one "yes", none "no". Poll No. 21 Winkler, with 244 available votes, polled two "yes" and none "no". Poll No. 16A, Horndean, with 187 available votes, polled one "yes" and one "no". Fifteen polls in that area, with a total available vote of 3,432, voted 40 "yes" and 40 "no". These people are a splendid type; there has been lack of leadership somewhere.
Just over a year ago the Minister of National Defence appealed to all federal members for assistance in recruiting throughout this country. What assistance did he obtain from his Manitoba colleagues in that respect? I venture to say his department received more active assistance from the lone opposition member than from all the government members from Manitoba.

3342	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Ross (Souris)
The Winnipeg Tribune of June 6, 1942, had an article entitled, "No Complacency". It stated:
The number of recruits for the armed services coming from Manitoba towns is a constant source of amazement. The record for enlistment in rural Manitoba has been consistently high ever since the war began, yet every call is quickly answered.
Here is a sample of what rural Manitoba is doing. The air force mobile recruiting party visited four communities and this is how the young men flocked to the colours:
Deloraine, population 850, joined up... 150 Killarney, population 1,000, joined up.. 250
Glenboro, population 500, joined up___	70
Souris, population 1,600, joined up.... '300 This rural response is the reason why Manitoba is at the top of the recruiting list for Canada with one volunteer for every twenty residents. It is also a clear sign that there is no complacency in the country.
The same might be said of the population of many other towns in southwestern Manitoba.
However, as a result of this there is a decided shortage of efficient farm labour. National selective service for any theatre of war would have avoided many of the conditions now prevailing in industry, agriculture and the armed forces in this respect. I have discussed this matter on previous occasions with both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). The Minister of Agriculture published a speech on September 12, 1941, as a press release from the bureau of public information, in which he stated:
If we are required to muster a million men for our armed forces we would still have seven million people left in Canada over sixteen years of age. These seven million, properly organized and determined to stand behind the armed forces, can operate all our farms, our factories and places of business, in a manner which will give us the production required.
The same minister during August, 1940, was Minister of National War Services when the registration of man-power of this country was made. During that period of almost two years, what has been done properly to organize the people of this nation? Speaking on June 9 I referred to the matter and pointed out that the Prime Minister made his man-power speech on March 24 about national selective service, but that to this date nothing has been done about applying it to agriculture. We are simply drifting into a hopeless muddle.
It may be argued that the voluntary system is obtaining sufficient men while our troops are not in battle, but I would urge the government not to wait until a military crisis is upon us so that again it will have to be said: "Too little and too late."

We have the report on the Canadian expeditionary force to Hong Kong. I do not wish to refer at any length to that, but there were some parts of the report not referred to when the Prime Minister put a portion on Hansard on June 5. On page 42 it is stated that:
. . . men without previous military experience served in the basic training centre for periods varying from three to eleven weeks.
Some had served only three weeks.
It was stated that:
These steps were taken with speed and secrecy. . . .
The Grenadier Guards were reinforced from military district No. 10. A number were taken from Dundum camp, military district No. 12. They ran around the country getting men who were untrained. On page 39 the report says:
Colonel Sutcliffe estimated on October 10 that between 150 and 200 additional men would be required.
And permission was obtained from headquarters to take these men. On page 45 it says:
On the whole matter I find there was no dereliction of duty or error in judgment from the mere fact that approximately 120 men were included in the expedition before they had completed their prescribed periods of training.
I have already found that the addition of these men did not impair the efficiency of the expedition nor did it constitute an injustice to these men themselves.
Would any ex-service man believe that untrained men taken under these conditions constituted no injustice?
On another page it states that they went without mechanical transport and other equipment; and the reason why they did not get at least a portion of their mechanical transport was that one of these controllers misunderstood orders and did not send it. I say to the country that this report, which suggests that it does not matter whether troops are trained or whether they have sufficient equipment, was a fine piece of whitewashing. Let us not be misled in this way at such a time; let us act immediately to have, on a basis of equality of sacrifice, armed forces with proper and sufficient reserves and equipment which will be second to none in the world. Let us raise those forces as they are raised in Great Britain and the United States of America to-day. Then we shall not have to hang our heads in shame, as many of us must do these days.
Perhaps we suffer from too much provincialism of the past. In my opinion we require in this country a federal system of education. In the past too much was left to provincial

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maclnnis
departments. I trust that we may study and appreciate the problems of the Canadian people irrespective of our racial antecedents. Canada has vast possibilities for the future if we win this war. Can we not discuss and deal with these matters as Canadians, from the Canadian viewpoint? If we do so, may I be so bold as to suggest, in view of what is happening to-day, that the manly course for the Prime Minister under these circumstances would be to hand over the reins of government to either the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and ask either of these hon. gentlemen to form a national government composed of the best and ablest men in Canada, representative of all shades of opinion, but united in the common, single purpose of waging a total war by a total effort. Canada is distinctly held back during these days by party limitations. The limitations of party government must be thrown off before the will of the Canadian people can be translated into more effective national action, which is so urgently needed at this time. I thought there was a great deal of merit in the appeal made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon to his compatriots in the province of Quebec, and I should like to join with him in that appeal. We should all try to solve the problems which are confronting us to-day by dealing with them as Canadians, irrespective of our past racial history, on the basis on which these matters have been dealt with by our great neighbours to the south. A great deal still can be accomplished if we go at it in the right manner.
The hopes of Canada now rest with the conscience of parliament. The people have spoken, and it is the business of their representatives to give effect to their voice. Surely members of parliament on the government side will not remain silent and unconcerned while the birthright of the young men who are now awaiting the zero hour in England is sold for a mere mess of political pottage.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we must all take our part in this debate according to the way we view what is happening in the world to-day. My first word will be that in my humble opinion this debate is the most important we have had in this house since September, 1939. It is important not only because of the conscription issue itself. I think the mere question of conscription for overseas military service is relatively unimportant in comparison with the stakes at issue in this world struggle in which we, together with the other free nations, are engaged. I believe that if we face the facts 44561-2121,
with minds as free as possible from prejudices both old and new, we shall find first that in each of the united nations the paramount need to defeat the axis powers has produced a degree of unity that is magnificently inspiring for the present and gives hope of great accomplishments for the future. I do not think it is necessary to draw to the attention of this house how a decade of struggle against a ruthless, cruel enemy has unified the warring factions of the sprawling population of China. We also have the example of how a realization of the dangers confronting them has for the time being almost obliterated class and party barriers in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and the United States. The right to criticize of course has not been relinquished, but it is exercised in such a way as not to interfere with the task at hand, the defeat of the enemy. That unity in some of these countries, however, was not gained without some persons, who for long had been high in the councils of the nation, having to step aside.
If we face the facts, I think the second thing we shall find is that where unity could not be achieved because of the selfish machinations of a privileged, profiteering class, and because of the loss of faith in democratic institutions by some sections of the working class, a great nation, France, lies prostrate under the nazi heel.
If we face the facts, I think the third thing we shall find is that for Canada the need for unity is just as important as it was in the case of the countries I have mentioned; and may I say again that it is important not only because of our part in this war but because it is necessary if we are to meet the problems which will confront us when peace is made.
One of the problems confronting us in Canada is how we are to bring about unity within the country itself. I believe the essentials to the creation of national unity in Canada are that the people everywhere should have a clear understanding of:
1.	Why we are in the war.
(2)	why and how we went into the war of our own free will, and
(3)	what we as a people expect to get out of the war.
The last and the first are particularly important, because unless we understand why we are fighting and what the results of our share in the fighting will be, or what the results of the sacrifices we are called upon to make will be, we cannot carry on with the enthusiasm and fortitude necessary in a struggle of this kind.
The reason why we have not the desired unity in Canada to-day is that no real

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maclnnis
effort has been made 'by the government to give the people an understanding of the three factors I have mentioned. There has been a holding back on the part of the government, a refusal to accept and proclaim the revolutionary nature of the war as a complete break with the political and economic policies of the last twenty-five years-policies which led inevitably and inexorably to war.
Last Thursday all hon. members listened to an eloquent and moving address by the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vereheres (Mr. Cardin). For myself, there was much in his speech with which I agreed, and I believe there was much with which we all agreed. I agreed with him when he condemned the government for lack of honesty with regard to the subject of conscription. I mentioned that matter myself in my speech on the address. As some other hon. members have quoted from other debates in this session, I crave the privilege of quoting a short paragraph from my speech on that occasion. I pointed out that, because of the way the plebiscite was introduced, in one part of the country it would be taken as a vote for conscription, and in another part it would be taken merely as a vote to relieve the government of any pledges which had been made. The group to which I belong proposed that in dealing with the question of conscription the people of Canada should have before them a clear and definite issue. It was with this in mind that I said, as reported at page 341 of Hansard:
The group with which I sit are, as we have already stated, in favour of a vote on the clear issue of conscription, because we believe it is the real issue confronting the people of Canada to-day. We favour a vote on two questions: (a) conscription of man-power; (b) conscription of material reosurces, industry and finance. If both questions were given to the people for endorsation or rejection, I feel convinced that they would approve both provided they were told it was necessary.
They were not told it was necessary. They are not being told to-day that it is necessary. The government is saying, "Give us the power, and when we think it is necessary we will put conscription into effect on the terms and conditions we think fit, without any reference whatsoever to parliament. We have asked the people to free our hands. We now ask you, parliament, to free our hands and let us carry on, as if parliament were not here at all." That is not good enough, in view of the past record of the government.
I fully agreed with the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vereheres when he said, or implied, that the cry for conscription of man-power, without regard to the nature of Canada's contribution to the total war plans of the

united nations, came mainly from a small group of profit-seekers. These people have been shouting for the conscription of manpower and the regimentation of labour almost ever since the war began. Yet they oppose every move which seeks not only to conscript, but to give the government definite and reasonable control over the material and financial resources of this country.
I have nothing but contempt for this group of short-sighted reactionaries in Canada, who are more ready even to sacrifice their own sons than to give up a tittle of their wealth,
* privilege and power. It was the refusal of similar reactionaries at the heart of empire to make any concessions to the colonial sections of the empire which has brought that empire to the very verge of dismemberment. That class of people has always acted too late.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
house rose at six o'clock I had made reference to the fact that there was a small group of people in this country who were calling for the conscription of men and for the regimentation of labour but were not prepared themselves to give up the smallest fraction of their wealth or privileges. A concrete example comes to my mind. I remember that one of the first of these gentlemen to call for the conscription of man-power was James Duncan who, just prior to the incident mentioned, had been deputy minister of national defence for air. He made the demand for conscription in a speech that was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of November 1, 1941, but just a short time before, this same James Duncan, when the Massey-Harris company called him, abandoned his important war post as deputy minister for air and went back to his private business. The men whom he would conscript, once they are called to their posts, stay at their posts for the duration. They cannot desert their posts whether family or business reasons call.
The hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) this afternoon referred in scathing terms to the control exercised by a small group of industrial and financial pirates, I think he called them, and gave it as his considered conviction that when this war was over, the power exercised by these gentlemen would be a thing of the past. I do not know where he got his information-possibly from the stars-but certainly he did not get it from

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maclnnis
a study of conditions as they are in Canada to-day because, if there is one thing that has been clear beyond anything else ever since this war began, it is that these people are becoming more and more powerful. I saw it put very nicely in the last issue of Maclean's magazine. A gentleman in business for himself and also occupying a high position with the government wrote from his own business office a letter to himself as a government official about some matter. Next morning he went to his government office and found the letter he wrote to himself waiting for him. Then as a government official he replied to himself as a business man, and then going back to his own office the next morning and getting the letter he had sent to himself, he was greatly pleased with the efficiency of government departments. That is what is happening, and I am afraid that the hon. member for Atha-baska is going to be greatly disappointed if he sticks to the notion that once this war is over, these gentlemen are going to let go their strangle-hold on the people of Canada.
I have already made reference to the speech made on Thursday last by the former Minister of Public Works and Minister of Transport (Mr. Cardin) and indicated some points in his speech with which I agree. I also agree with the hon. gentleman when he warned the house that the deletion of section 3 from the National Resources Mobilization Act means conscription for overseas service, in spite of all the sophistry of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). And not only that; it means conscription for overseas service without any further reference of the question to parliament. Further, I think the hon. gentleman was also on solid ground when he protested against the undemocratic procedure of conscription being imposed by the stealth and secrecy of order in council. From his long association with such methods his words should cariy weight with this house. In all of this serious criticism I think the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres was definitely in the right. But even before he spoke, on the same day, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of this group, had pointed out the same facts. We of this group I think may be pardoned if we feel perhaps gratified'-that is not quite the proper term at such a time as this, but I cannot think of a better one-that our criticisms and suspicions of the government's methods have been confirmed by one who himself has had so many years of experience in the cabinet.
There were, however, points in the exminister's speech with which I did not agree, with which, indeed, I must take issue. He
was seriously wrong, I think, when he implied that the support of English-speaking Canada for the war is mainly because of our British connection. I do not deny that there are small groups in this country to whom our British connection is sufficient reason for support in this or in any other war. There are similar people in all countries, but their kind is getting less and less each day. I think my hon. friend was wrong there, but there may be justification for his statement, and that justification lies in the fact that the government of which he himself has so recently been an influential member has fostered those ideas. I could give a thousand illustrations, as could any man in this house, of how such ideas have been spread and fostered by the present government-that is that Canada is at war because Britain is at war. But I think one will suffice-I believe, an outstanding one. Some months ago the Prime Minister published a book of his war speeches. The title of the book, "Canada at Britain's Side", is sufficient justification for the statement made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. That title to my mind is as good an expression of apron-clinging colonialism as any imperialist could wish for. Taken as the title of a collection of his war speeches by a man who, since the passing of the statute of Westminster, has continually reminded us of Canada's equality with Great Britain as a member of the British commonwealth of nations, it is bad enough; but when one learns that the title of the French edition of the same book is "Le Canada et la Guerre", which is, I believe, translated into English, "Canada and the War", the thing is beyond comprehension. But it does explain to some extent why to-day we have disunity in Canada. It is and has long been the accepted policy of this government to say one thing in the province of Quebec and another thing, though not always the same thing, in the other provinces. It depended upon whether they were going east or west. When they went west they were monetary reformers; when they came east they were the most orthodox of the orthodox.
I wish again to emphasize that the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is seriously wrong when he says that the people of English-speaking Canada, in giving support to the war, are motivated by emotion rather than reason. In saying that, he does Englishspeaking Canada a great injustice, and I do not think he wanted to do that.
I am of British stock. Usually when a person says that he follows it up by saying that he is proud of it. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres said the other day that such things

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maclnnis
were accidents, and I am willing to leave it at that; no one needs feel proud of an accident. My father came to this country over a hundred years ago. My mother's people have been in Canada for over a hundred and fifty years. In my love for Canada I yield place to no one. But for an intelligent man to-day love of country is not enough. One must love freedom. One must love humanity. One must love progress. One must love decency. These are the things which are involved in this struggle, and it is for these reasons that the people of my race have given and are giving all that they can. I, therefore, want to assure the hon member for Ricbelieu-Vercheres and my other French-Canadian friends in this chamber that I have, like many other Englishspeaking people, passed through many troubled days during the past seven or eight years. We saw the menace of fascism coming nearer and nearer. We saw the reactionaiy Tory government of Great Britain making concession after concession to the dictators of Rome and Berlin. We saw the government of Canada spinelessly following the vacillating footsteps of a Baldwin and a Chamberlain. We saw collective security sabotaged and aggressors appeased in the hope of saving for a little while longer the right of a privileged class to rule and exploit. For me, for hundreds, for hundreds of thousands of Canadians this war did not begin in 1939. It has been going on for years-in Abyssinia, in China, in Spain, where the strategy and the implements we find to-day on every war front had been used and tested and perfected and their deficiencies, if any; found out.
The people of English-speaking Canada may and do feel pride in the courage and determination which the people of Britain have shown since May, 1940, but we support the war because of the issues at stake. These issues can be put very briefly. We are fighting to. maintain the position won by us and others through years of sacrifice and struggle. We are also fighting to maintain the right of the common people to enlarge and enrich their lives by their own efforts, through their own organization, and to live under the rule of law. We of this group made that abundantly clear in the very first statement just before Canada's declaration of war, in the session of September, 1939. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) speaking for this group, said on that occasion, as reported in' Hansard, page 55:
* Nevertheless, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation recognizes that Canada is now implicated in a struggle which may involve the survival of democratic institutions. We consider that in the cause of the allied powers lies, a hope of building European peace on a
	.
more secure foundation because, in part at least, the people of Britain and France are waging a war against aggression.
We could not, Mr. Speaker, be unconcerned as to which side would win, and consequently we favoured Canada's participation in this war. In this war to-day we are proud to associate ourselves not only with Britain but with every free nation in the fight for survival, in the fight for freedom, and in the fight for the right to progress in our own way.
It is not necessary for me to elaborate on the causes which led to war; it is not a part of this debate. It is sufficient to note that the position of the world to-day is like that of a city in which dangerous gangsters are at large. No individual is safe until these gangsters are put under restraint. If the war has taught me anything, it is that the world to-day is a huge city. There is no longer isolation for nations any more than there is in an ordinary city isolation for the individual. The various nations are only the various sections of the city; the Chinese nation is the Chinese quarter, the Italian nation the Italian quarter, the British nation the British quarter, and so on. Consequently every nation must be concerned with what is taking place, and every nation must do its part to bring about a better and more orderly way of life.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, in common with the Labour parties of other sections of the commonwealth, has condemned British imperialism as vigorously as any other and perhaps more vigorously because we felt we had more right to do so. It is our belief, however, that the British commonwealth of nations as a league of self-governing, independent and equal partners will play an important part in the new world which will follow this war. I have stressed these points because I want to make it clear beyond the possibility of doubt why this group wants an all-out war effort.
We cannot, however, support the government in what it is now asking unless we get from the government some guarantee that will convince us that the sacrifice asked of the people will not be in vain. Past experience, as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) pointed out the other evening, is a justification for asking the government for these guarantees. For that reason, Mr. Speaker. I move, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy):
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor;
"this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that the principle of the bill before the house is inadequate and inequitable, permits the governor general in council to conscript men for overseas service without

Mobilization Act-Mr, Graham
reference to parliament, and is, therefore, contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
When, Mr. Speaker, you were giving the reasons the other evening for ruling out of order the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) Your Honour quoted an amendment moved by the present Prime Minister, who was leader of the opposition at the time, in 1934, that amendment being:
This house, while prepared to support legislation or assist in the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation.
This same right hon. gentleman is asking now, not that this house give him power over trade and commerce, over the natural products of the nation; he is asking parliament to give him power over the lives of the individuals in the nation. Surely, if the amendment I have just quoted was justified in 1934, when this house was dealing with inanimate things, the amendment I have just moved is much more justified on this occasion when we are dealing with the very lives of the people of the country. I submit that no better argument could be used for the appropriateness of this amendment.
There seems to be a wide difference of opinion even among members of the government as to whether or not this is a conscription bill. If I heard aright this afternoon, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said it was not; but the Prime Minister said the other evening very definitely that it was. I quote from page 3288 of Hansard of June 11:
Mr. Mackenzie King: What is my hon. friend talking about right now?

Mr. Mackenzie King:	Yes; the question of
overseas service is now before parliament.
But once this bill is passed, it will no longer be before parliament and all the power will be in the hands of the government. I noticed a quotation in a speech delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), at the legion convention in Winnipeg recently:
If the trumpet give an uncertain sound-who shall prepare himself to the battle?
By the sounds the trumpet is making I think it is badly cracked.
In the few moments left at my disposal there is another point I wish to make. I do so to support a statement I made a few minutes ago, that the policy of the members
of the government changes as they go east or west. In Ottawa it is, of course, stationary and absolutely reactionary. When my hon. friend was at the legion convention, speaking of course not as Minister of Pensions and National Health, but as a member of the Canadian Legion, he said:
You are to have a serious debate to-morrow morning on the conscription question. If I had my way, the first conscript in Canada would be money.

In the time allotted to me I propose to deal with some of the matters brought up by the leaders of the opposition parties in this house. Let me go further, because I think it is important. Williams, who had at that time I think become a member of his majesty's forces, challenged that convention to defeat him as leader on the ground that he supported the war effort of this country. If I may now continue, even as a war-time policy I think the argument is all against the suggestions of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. I do not believe that the leader of that party in this house or any of those who sit with him have any fixed conviction that there is any possibility now or in the near future of the adoption of the programme he suggests as the proper one for Canada to pursue. I think he would agree with that statement. If that be true, does he consider that he is adding to the efficiency of this country's war effort by saying, in effect, to the government, properly elected in a democratic manner by the Canadian people since the outbreak of the war to conduct the country's war effort, "we refuse to support any measure which this government presents unless they will accept the dictation of this party and impose, not only upon this parliament but upon the people of this country, state socialism", which he knows cannot come into existence now or in the near future?
I will go further. I have listened to my hon. friend speak highly-and in that I would join him-with regard to the leaders of the Labour party in the old land. He has often referred, and with approval, to the Hon. Ernest Bevin. Let me bring to the attention of the house the attitude of Mr. Bevin toward the war effort of Great Britain

Mobilization Act-Mr.. Graham
on an occasion of exact similarity to that which is now before this house. On December 4, 1941, the British House of Commons was discussing the extension of the selective service system to women. One Mr. Daggar moved an amendment, similar in its purpose but differently phrased from that* moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Let me read Mr. Daggar's resolution:
Mr. Daggar: I beg to move, in line 1, to leave out from the word "that" to end of the question, and to add instead thereof:
"This house, while assenting to the extension of the principle of compulsion to the man-power and woman-power still available, is of opinion that, in order to secure the full utilization of national resources in the war effort, it is essential that industries vital to the successful prosecution of the war, and especially transport, coal mining and the manufacture of munitions, should be brought under public ownership and control, and that the necessary legislation should be brought in as soon as possible."
I ask fhe house to notice this, that those who moved that resolution had the interests of the war effort at heart-and it is so stated in the wording of the resolution, because the first words are "while assenting to the extension of the principle".
The amendment attempted to be moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar starts off by saying that this bill be not now read a second time. In other words, it is a refusal to give any measure of support to the Prime Minister and the government who are charged with the task of carrying on this war effort.
What attitude did Mr. Ernest Bevin take with regard to Mr. Daggar's resolution? He took the attitude I would expect a great patriot would take. He spoke against it and succeeded in persuading the house that it was an improper resolution to bring before it. I not only quote him, but I could quote Mr. Shinwell who, I think my hon. friend would agree, is an ardent and enthusiastic socialist in the old country. He, too, in discussing the amendment admitted quite frankly that it was impossible to bring in such a transfer of management and ownership and control of the industries without creating such confusion and, shall I say, almost revolution in the country that it would so disturb the war effort as to be unwise. Let me quote his words, in dealing with all the avenues open to him: Another possibility is to take over all war production, including shipbuilding, and run it as a state affair, using the technical and administrative staffs and leaving questions of compensation to be determined at the close of the war. While this is consistent with the policy of the Labour party, it may be rejected because of the political disturbance it involves.
In order that I may assist the war effort, I want to draw to the attention of the house the difference between my hon. friend's party and those in Great Britain who are held up by my hon. friend for approval. They have been held up on more than one occasion. I would compare their attitude with that of hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party in this house, in moving the amendment they did.

I would invite the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, whose political capacity and whose power to assist the government in this war effort is very great, to forsake the opportunity to advance the fortunes of the political party to which he adheres, and to do as we on this side of the house are doing, namely, surrender for the moment, in the interests of the nation, the right to bring up controversial matters, which can be left until peace comes to us again.
Surely that is the attitude we have the right to ask of every hon. member in the house, when we examine the war situation as it is to-day. My own attitude in this matter is, I believe, very plain and, I hope, a patriotic one. If it becomes a necessity, and if I believe it will help the war effort of the country, I am prepared to conscript man-power for any purpose. If it becomes a necessity, and if I believe it will further the interests of the war effort of the country, I would conscript wealth of all kinds, both annual and accumulated. If it becomes a necessity, and if I believe that it will help the war effort of the country, I would conscript or compulsorily take over all of the industry needed to be taken over.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Why not concede us the same right?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I go further than the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-at least, if I understand their policy as that enunciated last Thursday by its leader. If it were a necessity and if I thought it in the interests of the war effort of this country, I would conscript labour, f noticed particularly that my hon. friend did not suggest that to this house, when he mentioned conscription of man-power.
On the other hand, if, after giving due consideration to each, and after having, I hope, obtained the information I require from the sources which would have that information, I

Mobilization Act-Mr, Grahtfm
find that that is not a necessity, and that it would not help the war effort, I would vote against any such measure. I believe that is the simple attitude which we can all adopt, because it is the one which holds out the only present hope of speedy victory.
It seems to me that if we could imagine the people of Canada all gathered together in this House of Commons to-night, and suddenly the gentleman usher of the black rod, or some other official, came and announced that the Japanese were at the west block and the Germans at the east block, we would speedily forget all of our political futures, all our political plans and hopes, and would join together under the best leadership available for the purpose of meeting the enemy. I will admit (hat that illustration is somewhat extreme, but I submit that the real and actual situation justifies the illustration. Inasmuch as the Japanese have invaded the Aleutian islands off our western coast, and the German submarines have entered the St. Lawrence river, I think my illustration is not too farfetched. We as members of the House of Commons have a common duty to perform in supporting the government, as well as the duty each one has in carrying out his share of the war effort.
We speak of the patriotism and the sacrifice of the young men who are called upon to fight in the front line. In my day and age we were called upon to fight in the war of 1914-18. The young men and the young women of this day are called to fight in a much more terrible and more serious war in every respect, so far as the results which may possibly flow from it are concerned. If we are asking those young men to risk the sacrifice of their physical lives, then surely it is not asking too much of hon. members to ask us to place upon the altar of this our native land our political lives, and to consecrate ourselves to the duty of giving to this government, the chosen of the people, every possible measure of support, so that we can bring victory- certain, and as soon as possible.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke this afternoon he said that the leader of this group had stated, when speaking on this measure, that we had taken a stand against either public ownership or control of industry. Therefore, in order to set the record straight in the matter I should like to quote what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) did say in regard to industry. I am sure, had the Minister of Agriculture read the speech, he would not have made the statement he did make.

The speech of the hon. member for Lethbridge is found at page 3273 of Hansard, and from it I quote the following:
Nevertheless this group conceives a state in which industry shall do what the state tells it to do. Why should such an outrage as has been referred to already, in the Dumart plant, continue unchecked? If an industry simply refuses to obey the directions of government, then the government without hesitation should force it to sell its shares to the government or to some other industry which would be prepared to obey the government's will and fall into cooperation. There are other forms of compulsion which could be used. As a result of the application of these devices it would be possible to conscript completely industry in this country, which means to bring it under control so that it will cooperate with the state for the people of the state.
In passing, I should like to stress the fact that this group has consistently advocated the control of industry by government.
To-day it is so obvious that unless we defeat the enemy overseas we shall have to defeat him at home on the American continent, that no sound argument can any longer be presented that Canada ought not to participate to the greatest possible degree in the overseas conflict. That conclusion having been reached, it becomes a question of what is the most equitable way of calling up men for military service. The voluntary system to-day as imposed by this government is a policy of flogging the willing horse. It is neither just nor efficient. A continual appeal is made to a person's sense of patriotism, to his conscience, with the result that the entire personnel of some families is wiped out, while other families make no contribution whatsoever. This policy has been maintained largely no doubt as a matter of political expediency. I would call it appeasement in its very worst form, and appeasement invariably fails. If the objective is, as we have been told, national unity, I think we can say that the government has failed to achieve its objective. If the objective has been unity within the Liberal party, I think one can also say, after listening to some of the speeches that have been made in this house, that appeasement has failed even in that direction.
If the war were a minor operation, or if we had many men wishing to volunteer for foreign service, then I would say that the voluntary system would be satisfactory. So long as we had plenty of men in this country clamouring to be allowed to go overseas I would say that the voluntary system was satisfactory. But as soon as you had a situation where you had to badger men and resort to various questionable practices in order to induce or coerce men to enlist, I would say that the voluntary system had failed and that the time for conscription had come.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Quelch
In war-time it is absolutely essential that we should at all times strive for the greatest degree of equality of service and sacrifice. It may not be possible to achieve that objective. It cannot be achieved, I admit, 100 per cent, but that does not for one minute excuse the government for failing to strive continually to reach that objective to the greatest degree possible, and I would say that is equally true whether we have a voluntary or a compulsory service for overseas. Surely those who enlist on a voluntary basis have just as much right to demand equality of service and sacrifice as those who are conscripted, and I would say that no man should be asked to give his life for his country either voluntarily or by compulsion unless at the same time those who stay at home are prepared to assume their full responsibility in that effort. Just to show that we have been quite consistent in our attitude regarding the war since its declaration, I would quote briefly what I said on September 11, 1939, when we were discussing the appropriation bill. It will be found at page 99 of Hansard. I said:
In time of war it becomes necessary to call upon certain people to be willing to sacrifice their lives. It becomes necessary for some people to make that supreme sacrifice. It is necessary for others to suffer mutilation of the body. Is it asking too much to ask people remaining in Canada, in comparative safety, to be willing to sacrifice the major portions of their incomes? Is that asking too much, at a time when we are asking other people to sacrifice their lives? I say we have every right to demand that those who remain in safety he prepared to sacrifice the major portion of their incomes, that they be permitted to retain only that portion which is necessary for the maintenance of a moderate standard of living.
Again:
We believe in utilizing the Bank of Canada so that we may create the necessary financial credits and currency, combined with definite price regulation so as to obviate any serious rise in prices. We would advocate, further, steeply graded income and profits taxes. We maintain, further, that the only possible justification for borrowing is when our need for goods is greater than our ability to produce them. That condition of course requires external borrowing. We see absolutely no justification for internal borrowing.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would say that when the men return from overseas they should not be called upon to make any further sacrifice. When they have fought this war and won it they will have made all the sacrifices they should be called upon to make, without being called upon, when they return, to start to help paying the cost of the war. That is our responsibility now.
There would be no question of our overseas forces having to pay the cost of this war had
there been adopted from the outset, as we were led to believe would be adopted, a strictly pay-as-you-go policy. But to say to the men now overseas or in the active service forces: "We asked you to go without that guarantee, but we will not allow reinforcements to be conscripted without it", would in my opinion be a betrayal of our men overseas. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with those who say that we must vote against this bill until the government have adopted their particular brand of conscription of wealth. Furthermore, I consider that the plebiscite vote was a direct mandate to the government for the introduction of the bill now before us. Whether or not we have conscription for overseas makes no difference so far as the immediate conscription of the industrial and financial resources of the nation are concerned. Failure to do this means the loss of -morale, and the loss of morale may easily mean the loss of the war.
There is much that the people have to do in the line of duty. But that is not enough. For an all-out war effort people must be prepared to go beyond the line of duty. However, before you can expect to develop that spirit, before you can expect to instil a greater esprit de corps among the people, you must convince them not merely that you are fighting to defeat Hitlerism, which is simply a means to an end but that the real end in view is to introduce into the world a new social order based upon true Christian principles. As the Prime Minister, however, has said on several occasions, unless that new social order is well on its way before the end of the war, we might well look for that new order in vain.
Speak to the people on the streets; speak to the men in the army; speak to the men on the production lines, and what do you find? You find they are fearful. Fearful of what? Fearful of what is going to happen to them at the end of the war. The depression years from 1930 to 1939 are all too fresh in their memory. They remember the hundreds of thousands of men who were wandering across Canada looking for work, hundreds of whom were arrested on a vagrancy charge when their only crime was that they were looking for a job. They are wandering to-day what is going to happen when half a million men come back from overseas and when one million people now in the war industries are thrown out of a job upon the conclusion of the war. That is not a healthy state of mind for the people of any nation to be in, and so I believe it is high time for the Prime Minister to tell the people in- unmistakable terms, and assure them of it so that
Mobilization Act-Mr. Quelch

they can be certain of it beyond the shadow of a doubt, that a new social order will be brought in at the conclusion of the war. Promises such as those made by ministers sitting over there are not enough.
I remember that the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), speaking this afternoon, said that people should not be doubtful on this question. He said we are told that there will be a new social order. He said we have had the Atlantic charter. But I would remind the hon. member that, when I was overseas in the last war, we also listened to promises. Members of the government came to us in Prance and told us what would be done; we were fighting to make the world safe for democracy; this was a war to end wars, and everyone when he returned to Canada would be guaranteed a job and his family looked after. Were those promises kept? If promises to the soldiers in the last war were not kept, have we any reason to expect a better fate for the vague promises which are being made to-day? I do not think so.
So I would say that, before calling upon the people to make any greater sacrifices than they have already made-we are led to believe that further impositions will be announced in the coming budget, and the conscription of manpower will mean even greater sacrifices-the government of Canada should issue a declaration of principles for a Canadian charter. In other words, let them issue a declaration which will apply the Atlantic charter to Canada, and show how it will work, especially with regard to sections 4, 5 and 6. Take the section which . says that the nations of the world shall have free access to the raw materials of the world and that all peoples of the world shall be guaranteed freedom from fear and want and freedom from war. I believe that if the government were to issue a declaration such as I suggest and make it clear how the Atlantic charter will be applied to Canada, a long step would have been taken to build up the type of morale which is so necessary in war time.
I want to give a few examples of what the government might tell the people of Canada at this time in order to build up confidence. May I here remark that if such a declaration were issued, it would not be necessary to hire cheer leaders such as Mr. Hirst to go and try to build up the morale of the aircraft workers.
Let the Prime Minister tell the people of this country that the policy of not allowing financial restrictions to impede our war effort will apply equally to our post-war reconstruction period.
Let the Prime Minister say, giving it the widest possible publicity, that anything which can be achieved in the physical sense to bring

in a new social order will be made financially possible. I am satisfied that in that event the morale of the Canadian people would be greatly improved. I am somewhat doubtful whether the Prime Minister would be prepared to make such a statement.

I do not believe the people will ever be satisfied to be told again that they have to go on relief because there is not enough money to put them to work. Having seen that we can spend not only hundreds but thousands of millions of dollars for war, they are not going to be willing to have their sons wander from one end of the country to the other looking for work because the government says that there is no money available.

Mr. Speaker, I have said that I bow to your ruling.
Before I mentioned the billion dollar gift I was stressing the fact that if we are going to call upon the people of this nation to make further sacrifices, it is absolutely essential that we take steps to build up morale. I want to explain and stress how necessary it is that certain declarations shall be made to the people in order to build up the type of morale necessary to make them willing to undergo these sacrifices. I suggest that if the Prime Minister would explain to the people that by the end of this war Canada will be wealthier than it has ever been before, due to the fact that we shall have a greater plant capacity, and more skilled labour than we ever had, it will be merely a question of applying that skilled labour to our idle resources in order to give to the Canadian people the highest standard of living they have ever had; and if due publicity were given to that statement, that also would help to build up morale. I stress this point, because time and again I have read predictions that we are going to be poor at the end of this war and that it will be necessary to tighten the belts of the people to pay for it.
Anybody who studies this question knows that such a statement is unsound, and that in reality we shall have more wealth than we ever had before. I do not believe it is a good thing to cause loss of morale by making people believe that when this war is over they will undergo another depression. Yet we are being continually warned about another depression at the end of this war, without the smallest reason for such an assumption.

I am satisfied that if, following up a declaration of that kind, the government would take immediate action to prove to the people that they are going to do everything in their power to bring about greater equality of service and sacrifice, they would go a long way toward restoring public confidence that a new social order is in reality in the making. As an immediate proof of our sincerity, let the government take the following steps to demonstrate to the people now that we mean what we say when we assert that a new social order will be brought in.
