Yes. That amendment is:
That all the words after the word "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor: this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that the principle of the bill before the house is inadequate and inequitable, permits the governor general in council to conscript men for overseas service without reference to parliament, and is therefore contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
The amendment declares that the present measure is inequitable and inadequate, and the hon. member for Vancouver East stressed the fact and showed why it was inadequate. He stressed the fact that it was inadequate because it did not provide for conscription of wealth, and he also pointed out that it would be necessary to revise our whole system of taxation. To that extent I agree with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, that when we are calling upon people to make the supreme sacrifice the very least we can do is to ask others to be prepared to sacrifice the major portion of their incomes.

The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, I believe, suggested a ceiling of from $12,000 to $15,000. I am satisfied that if people could be guaranteed an income of $15,000 during the war, making allowance for a steeply graduated income tax from the low income brackets up to $15,000, such people should indeed consider themselves lucky. I have often stated in this house that if any man can go through this war and maintain his pre-war savings intact and maintain a fair standard of living, being no worse off at the end of the war than at the start, he should consider himself indeed fortunate and should not be allowed to accumulate large holdings of bonds, as is being done at the present time. I believe also that in order that we may have a more equitable condition in this country, a comprehensive programme of social services should be introduced. When we heard the programme referred to by Mr. Nash, and when we read of various other programmes of social services in other countries throughout the world, I think we should justly feel that there is much to be done in that regard in Canada.
I believe that the soldiers from the last war can justly demand that greater consideration be given their problems in the future. When we take into consideration that widows of disability pensioners to-day are still in many cases on relief, receiving no pension, and when we remember that many a soldier settler from the last war is living to-day in poverty and destitution, I think we can feel that much can be done with regard to these men.
All the things to which I have referred should be put into operation at the very earliest possible date, and I submit that the government should give a definite assurance to the people that better conditions will be brought about at the end of the war. The men in the active service forces are entitled to that assurance now; but the members of the group to which I belong are not going to refuse to agree to the removal of the overseas limitation from the mobilization bill until that is done. The plebiscite gives the government a free hand in that regard, and the fact that we are doing the men overseas an injustice now by not having conscription of wealth is no reason why we should add to that injustice by refusing to guarantee them reinforcements for overseas service.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last February, I opposed in this house, to the indignation of certain people in my province, the holding of the. plebiscite foreshadowed in the speech

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
from the throne. I held that the government, commanding an unprecedented majority in the house, would thereby merely give ground in the face of a group less interested in national unity than in the passing of conscription for overseas service. I have not changed my views on the subject. I also held that in the event of an affirmative vote the pressure exerted by certain cabinet ministers and members, as well as by the apposition and the imperialists and their newspapers, would be so strong, so hard to counter that the government could not long refrain from resorting to such conscription. I predicted moreover that the plebiscite would inevitably lead to overseas conscription, and that such a measure would destroy national unity and hamper our war effort.
The plebiscite was held. Discussion on the subject was not uniform in tenor throughout the country. In every province but Quebec, the need of a total war effort was stressed to the people. The speeches given by certain ministers are ample evidence that they considered conscription for overseas service as the natural corollary of an affirmative vote. And the opposition shared their view.
In Quebec, an afljrmative reply was sought on the basis that such a vote would prevent conscription. Quebec voted in the negative. Had Quebec voted otherwise, are we not justified in presuming, at the present rapid pace of events, that Bill No. SO would have been introduced on the very evening of the vote?
The very next day the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was already asking the government- to act. And now, hardly seven weeks after voting day, the measure is under discussion. Bill No. 80, if passed, will establish the principle of conscription for overseas service. Apparently the measure is considered urgent!
Mr. Speaker, I shall speak my mind freely, for I am conscious that in doing so I am fulfilling my duty. I oppose Bill No. 80 and shall vote against it. In February, I voted against the plebiscite which I termed mere camouflage; to-day I oppose this measure which proves to me how right I was in condemning the plebiscite. Bill No. 80 is a piece of anti-national legislation because its [DOT]passing will imperil if not destroy this embryo of unity to which years of understanding and concessions had begun to give shape. The measure is useless, Mr. Speaker, if it is true that the voluntary enlistment system is adequate for our needs, and it would be nothing short of superfluous to demonstrate that only such a system can
give to our war effort its maximum efficiency. And if I oppose this bill after opposing the plebiscite, if the province of Quebec shares the same view, if all those who voted negatively think the same way, it is certainly not because I, any more than they, am opposed to the war effort or a traitor to the British crown, as the imperialistic press would have us believe.
The province of Quebec voted no on the plebiscite. This she was entitled to do, as were all voters in Canada, French Canadian or otherwise, who shared the same opinion. At the moment, however, it would appear that the imperialists and their newspapers are reserving their fire for Quebec and Quebec only.
I do not countenance separatist views, Mr. Speaker. I consider that Quebec cannot live apart in this confederation, no more than any of our other provinces could. I do not favour nationalism based on racial prejudice, for my conception of true nationalism embraces the entire country.
But the time has arrived, I believe, to restate certain questions. This in no way applies to the English-speaking voters in my constituency who, while holding their own views, have long since learned to respect their French-speaking fellow citizens, nor to those English Canadians who have unceasingly cooperated with their fellow citizens of French descent in the moulding of a greater and better Canada. Rather does it apply to a group of Canadians, mostly by adoption, whose sympathies are not here but across the seas. To them I say that national unity has always been maintained in this country, not because all provinces made equal concessions but because Quebec was the only one to make them. Her kindness, tolerance and good will were well known. Because she never refused, the imperialists made hay while the sun shone. Because she granted their every request, they paid her homage; less because she deserved it than because she placed no obstacle in their path to domination and autocracy. Now that Quebec has voted no on the plebiscite, she has immediately become the unworthy province, the treacherous province, the one to be feared.
We are little understood, Mr. Speaker. It is no doubt due to the negative answer given by Quebec on the plebiscite that Mr. Carson, made the following statement at the eighty-third annual meeting of the Grand Lodge for western Ontario, held in Toronto on May 27 last:
As members of the Orange order, we are not willing to see this great country pass under the control of eueh a reactionary power as the
3358	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
Roman Catholic church, of that kind of a Catholic church which is to be found in French Canada. The fullest consideration should be given to the steps necessary to meet this insidious menace coming from the province of Quebec and which threatens the British and protestant character of this dominion.
Such a statement, Mr. Speaker, proves both the blind fanaticism of its author and his ignorance of Canadian history. The reverend Mr. Shields, who should have been interned long since, for he has more than any one Canadian raised prejudices to foster antagonism toward Quebec on the part of the Englishspeaking provinces, is unceasing in his attacks upon our province, our clergy and our institutions. Is all this conducive to national unity? Is national unity fostered in any way by the insults coming from the imperialistic press in this country and having Quebec for target? Are all these people ignorant of the fact that no other province shows greater tolerance, greater benevolence, yea, greater love for minorities than does the province of Quebec. This disposition has its root in our hospitable nature, our wish for good understanding, our spirit of charity in keeping with the teachings of our clergy. We have no reason to be ashamed of our tolerance toward minorities. They who would sow the seed of prejudice should at least have some knowledge of the history of the country in which they live: they might mend their ways. If there are extremists in my province, I certainly condemn them as I condemn extremists in other provinces. If others knew us better they would soon find out that we have never ceased to be loyal subjects of the British crown.
Of course, French Canadians will always remain a minority in this country. Even if a generous birth-rate is constantly increasing their number, immigration will always be a compensating factor. Besides, they do not seek to become masters in the land, but they do hold to their fair share of sunlight, being fully convinced that they had something to do with settling and developing this country.
We were the first to come here. When England, in 1760, took from France one of the fairest colonies of that time, we accepted defeat, but we did not accept to be deprived of our rights. If I have reason to state to-night that England granted privileges to my people,
I know I make no mistake in stating that even in practising our religion and in speaking our tongue we have never been guilty of treason to the British crown.
Moreover, history is witness to our cooperation. Less than fifteen years after the conquest, in 1775, French Canadians stood by England^ at the behest of Monsignor Briand, then Bishop of Quebec. Our people turned a deaf ear to the English from New England seeking 
their own independence, yea, even to France who, bent on revenge, had joined the revolutionary cause.
The -war of 1812 between England and the United States furnished another proof of our loyalty. The third route of invasion-through the Richelieu valley leading to Montreal- was defended by our own people. Led by de Salaberry at Chateauguay, outnumbered fifteen to one, so staunch and so brave was their resistance that the American army was forced to retreat.
Should one claim that in 1837 there was a revolt in Quebec, I would reply that this revolt was, in its way, a demand for the recognition of disregarded rights, similar in every respect to that which Ontario loyalists organized about the same time when they went on to attack the Toronto city hall for the selfsame purpose of obtaining redress. It is possible to condemn certain excesses, to condemn certain attitudes, without condemning at the same time the misuse of power which brought them on.
Was there in 1918 any regiment which brought more glory to itself than the 22nd, exclusively made up of Canadians of French descent? And in the present war, have French Canadians been remiss in their duty, have they refused to do their part? How many of our people are now under arms on active service? Have we refused to cooperate in any war service? Have we declined to help England and the united nations? Have we been opposed to the war effort?
And, in the mind of certain people, Quebec would represent a threat to the British empire, to the security of the country! They would tag us as anti-British because we decline to accept the principle of conscription for overseas service. I should be a traitor to the empire because, as a Canadian, I condemn a measure destined to destroy national unity in Canada, a British country. A traitor, because in a free country I enjoy the right of holding an opinion freely and because I state it? Not traitors, Mr. Speaker, but authentic Canadians, for our first love goes to our own country.
I intend voting against Bill No. 80 because it confers upon the government unlimited powers. We are asked by the proposed legislation to remove section 3 from the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, a clause which prevented the government from conscripting men for service outside Canada. If this bill is adopted the government will be authorized to send troops to any part of the world. One might object that although the government will be free to exercise this power,

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
it is possible that they may never do so. If the government do not avail themselves of this authority or intend to do so, what purpose will this bill serve save that of dividing Canada. for years to come? If the government does avail itself of this authorization, will the consequences be less serious? I consider that voting for this bill is equivalent to giving the government a blank cheque; I feel that such a procedure is fraught with danger or, even reprehensible in private life, it is no less so in public affairs. Once article 3 is struck out, the government, in possession of sufficient power, will be in a position to adopt conscription, by order in council, at any time, without consulting parliament. I protest against this abusive use of authority with added1 vehemence due to the fact that the trainees under the 1940 act will immediately become subject to be sent overseas to any part of the world; I protest against this abuse of power, because we have no right to conscript for other fronts trainees who have been drafted on the promise that their energies would be expended for the defence of Canada only.
This is probably the last opportunity we will have of denouncing conscription for overseas. This method is repellent to our legitimate pride. We of Quebec are averse to any idea of compulsion in the line of sacrifice and duty. During the last three centuries, our ancestors fought the Iroquois and then the forest and the unproductive soil; they dedicated themselves to the accomplishment of this momentous task; their efforts were put forth not so much for their own sake as for the sake of the generations to come. This fact binds us so closely to the Canadian soil that we cannot conceive, even for a moment, that our country might extend outside of Canada. Could it be within the power, even of imperialists, to sever us from our soil, to which we are so deeply attached? For our Canadian homeland, for its defence, we shall stop at no sacrifice, we shall give our last dollar, our life blood, even our lives.
The people of Quebec are averse to conscription for overseas because they have not forgotten 1917. Our small people may have struck from their memory many facts that have deeply wounded them at various times, but they have never and will never forgot that in 1917, conscription was a political manoeuvre directly applied against them and their province. The mistakes against Quebec and its people during the last war have been both serious and exasperating, for the enlistment officers have systematically refused to acknowledge the pride felt by a sensitive ethnical group on account of their special characteristics.
Once again, conscription would be adopted by imperialists, enforced by them and used to their selfish ends. What measure of fairness could we expect when so much unfairness has already been perpetrated? How much consideration could Quebec command? How much consideration could the large families command-and they are all in Quebec-when, at the present time, the methods of enlistment for the defence of our country, do not take this fact into account?
Conscription for service overseas would be a colossal mistake; it would even be a disgrace for our territorial defence forces. Would Canada then enjoy sufficient protection? Is she in a position to cope with an invasion threat when her vast territory borders on two oceans? Has enough thought been given to her position? What has Australia done? During two years she has sent the very best of her soldiers to battlefronts all over the world; to-day, left without enough troops to face the danger, she is calling for reinforcements. What a sad mistake and also what a lesson!
Conscription for overseas service would be a crime because it is unnecessary. The ministers have told us many times during the last six months that the voluntary system of enlistment was adequate. Has there been any sudden failure of that system? Has it been advertised as much as it could have been? Has every effort been made to ensure its success? Have not certain imperialistic circles endeavoured to hinder the voluntary system of enlistment? Have they not dealt with it carelessly, for the sole purpose of forcing the government to resort eventually to conscription? If the voluntary system does not yield enough men, let the government take whatever means may be necessary to stimulate it. Let the government increase the allowances to the volunteers' dependents. Let them give more opportunities for promotion, so that military life may become a permanent career instead of a temporary avocation. Let voluntary service be made interesting, and the voluntary system will be adequate. The expenditure of a few more millions in order to ensure the success of the voluntary system would not be extravagant at a time when billions of dollars are being spent. What if the government were to pay a few more millions in dependents' allowances to maintain the voluntary system, which is the basis of our national unity and our war effort?
The champions of imperialism, be they tories or grits, want conscription for overseas service. They want it and they brush aside every objection. Remind them that the population of this country is only 11 million, that is three persons per square mile, as compared with 43 in the United States and 489 in England,
3360	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
they still want conscription. Tell them that out of five and a half million men in Canada, two million are under 17 or over 70, they want it just as badly. Tell them that over a million men are under arms, that there remain perhaps one million and a half for the factories, and the farms, without taking into account those who are unfit for military service, or those who are sick or crippled, they still want conscription. Why do they want it? Could they explain why they want it?
But we do know why we do not want conscription for overseas service. We do not want it because, in our opinion, that kind of conscription is more for the defence of the empire than for the defence of my country. My opposition to this bill is not a protest against Canada's war effort, but a protest against imperialism which seeks to dictate a policy to my country. History repeats itself. During each war, the champions of imperialism display more love for England than for Canada, and that provokes us. In this war, despite the fact that in 1940 all political parties stated their opposition to conscription for overseas service, the same imperialistic group from Toronto, the same small clique reappears on the scene. We are against that kind of conscription just as Australia, South Africa and Northern Ireland have opposed it. Why should we, as Canadians, accept it? Is there a province of Quebec in any of those countries?
We are primarily in favour of a truly Canadian war effort. Of course we are willing to help the allies win this war. We have spent huge sums, we have contributed in many ways, we have even made an outright gift of one billion dollars-or nearly $100 for each citizen of this country-as a further evidence of our sincerity. In those staggering expenditures, which are perhaps larger, in proportion to our population, than those of Great Britain or the United States, we French Canadians have also had a part. We have in this war shouldered the burden of taxation, accepted our share of the common sacrifices as well as every restriction, contributed in every field of the war effort-army, navy and air force-our voluntary and unstinted cooperation. What we have been asked to do we have done. We have contributed to all war services. The national debt is growing to such a size that perhaps we will never get out of it. Along with all other Canadians, we have not stayed behind. But the constituency of Terrebonne and its member will never agree to such a useless, autocratic and antinational measure as conscription for overseas service.
I will vote against the bill. I have been elected to do my duty and so I will. But I have a right to ask myself: "Whither the 
Liberal party?" Owing to its wild nonsense and its misuse of authority in 1917, the Conservative party could only be a party which lacked life-giving breath; in the province of Quebec it has long been dead and cremated. The Liberal party had always preached a doctrine which took its inspiration at the very source of the true Canadian spirit. People had put their trust in it. My constituents had faith in the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Even to-day, they cannot imagine the Liberal party obliterating from our history with a stroke of the pen all its political prestige and disrupting this national unity which has always been its objective and its ideal; my constituents cannot conceive of the Prime Minister destroying or allowing to be destroyed, for the benefit of an imperialist clique, the essentially Canadian policies which he had championed and out of which he derived the sway and brilliancy of his parliamentary career; after so many years of boundless confidence, they feel repugnance to ask themselves: "Now that the old parties have deceived us, whom shall we trust?"
They will be told that the bill is but a confirmation of the general result of the plebiscite, that it does not entail conscription, that the governmen/t will impose conscription only if circumstances require, and may perhaps never do so. Unfortunately, my constituents no ' longer believe such promises.
As a member of this house, as a citizen of this country, I do not look upon myself as a French Canadian but simply as a Canadian.
I am a Canadian who speaks French. A Roman Catholic Canadian. The fact that I speak French and that I am a Catholic does not prevent my loving Canada and admiring Great Britain. But my first duty is to my country. I want the allies to win, I favour help to Great Britain and the united nations in the form of money, food, munitions and volunteers but I deny imperialism the right to thrust orders and leadership upon us. In this most solemn hour of its history, I feel that I am serving, not betraying my country, in voting against this measure of conscription for overseas which, in addition to doing a disservice to the allies, will make Canada a hotbed of mistrust, sterile wrangling, fruitless effort and sham cooperation. What mischievous blows the imperialist coterie has dealt our war effort.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter which is now before the house is so serious and important that it is our bounden duty to discuss it in all possible moderation, without bitterness or rancour, but solely from a national stand-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Durocher
point, taking into account the war effort we have already accomplished and what we were planning to do before the government introduced the proposed amendment for the repeal of section 3 of the mobilization act of 1940.
As we all know, that section empowers the government to require persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces only within Canada and its territorial waters. It was passed only after long discussions and in order to meet the wishes of the various elements in the Canadian parliament, and its purpose was to safeguard our national unity.
That act seemed to appease all minds and it stimulated in no small degree our war effort as regards our production, which was so much needed in Europe. It has been said on various occasions that we should have a total war effort. May I say at this time that however great our effort may have been so far, it could have been still greater if our factories had been allowed to produce to their utmost capacity. Unfortunately, they have been prevented from doing so, against our own will, for well known reasons which I deem better not to mention in this house, but which, nevertheless, discredited our war effort in Quebec even though we were in no way responsible. If the proposed amendment is passed, shall not the door be opened wide to conscription for overseas service, a policy which we have always opposed? If the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will permit me, I should like to quote the following excerpt from his radio address of April 7, 1942:
The pledge not to impose conscription, as every one knows, /was the result of Canada's experience in the last war. The way in which conscription was then introduced, and the way it was enforced, gave rise to bitter resentment. Moreover, events proved that conscription in the last war had little or no military value.
The pledge not to impose conscription for service overseas was given in order to maintain the unity of Canada. Without this assurance, I do not believe that parliament would have given, as it did, prompt and wholehearted approval to Canada's entry into the war.
Do we now intend to destroy this national unity so persistently advocated and to dampen the enthusiasm which has never faltered from the very beginning?
Further, the Prime Minister goes on to say:
The truth, of course, is that our army to-day is just as large as it would have been if conscription for overseas had been adopted.
If our war effort has in no way been limited by our not applying conscription, why not, as the saying goes, leave well enough alone? If the voluntary system has given such satisfactory results, for Heaven's sake, let us keep it, let us improve it if we can, but let us not spoil through any legislation or any amendment of an existing statute the good effects of the present system.
Throughout the campaign preceding the plebiscite vote, the Prime Minister, the ministers from Quebec as well as those from the other provinces and the members of parliament almost to a man unequivocally stated that the question of the plebiscite was in no way linked up with that of conscription. Nevertheless, as was so well stated by the former Minister of Public AVorks (Mr. Cardin) in his speech of the 11th instant, on the very day after the vote, even before the votes had been counted, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) rose in the house and made the following statement to be found on page 1921 of Hansard for April 28, 1942. I quote:
Now there is no stumbling block, real or imaginary, to total war. The hour has struck when every human and material resource must be mobilized for war service. Parliament now is free to act-there are no fetters upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or his government.
The leader of the opposition, however, had stated some time before in the house that it was impossible for him to put conscription on the banner of the Conservative party because that measure was not popular; he stated also that he had received numerous letters from mothers stating that they had not raised their sons to have them conscripted and this explains how it was that a movement was on foot, a few days later, to oust him out as leader of the opposition. This statement has displeased the ultra-imperialist members of his party.
We have also the oft repeated statements of the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National War Services and others, setting forth officially that the voluntary enlistment system is giving fully adequate results. If we accept these statements as being made in good faith, why are we called upon now to strike out of the National Resources Mobilization Act the only clause which enabled us to make certain pledges and declarations to the voters at the last election? I well remember having had the honour of greeting in my constituency, during the electoral campaign of March 1940, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, then Minister of Justice, who repeated the following statement which I quote:
I shall never be a member of a cabinet which introduces a measure calling for conscription for overseas service.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Durocher
This statement was repeated by every minister and member of the house who took part in the campaign in Quebec. We made the most solemn pledges to our electors and only they could free us from our obligations. And if the purpose of the plebiscite is being deliberately distorted to-day as an expression of public opinion in favour of conscription for overseas service, the only ones who are in a position to accept such a verdict are the members whose constituents recorded a majority of affirmative votes. What of the others? Like most of the Quebec members, they have not been released from their pledges. The voters of Quebec have once again shown most clearly their unalterable opposition to any amendment to the present legislation which would empower the cabinet to impose at discretion, by order in council and without consulting parliament, that conscription for overseas service which has been held up to us as a bogey for over twenty-five years by all political parties without exception.
We are being asked to expand our war effort in Canada, to furnish more airplanes, more ships and more munitions. How can we possibly do this if the labour necessary to such an end is conscripted from our plants? Let us not forget that we are already exempting farmers' sons, teachers, certain classes of students, the clergy and conscientious objectors, fishermen and lumbermen. Does this then mean that our cities will be called upon to supply all the men needed in the armed forces? Does it mean that conscientious objectors, who are able to bear arms, can invoke the privileges granted to them by the country and take refuge behind i principle, in order not to contribute to the var effort in the same measure as the rest of their fellow citizens?
No group or section of this house have attempted to influence my stand concerning this matter. Already at the partial election held in Saint James constituency, in 1939, as well as during the 1940 campaign, I stated unequivocally and without restriction, that, confident in my leaders, I opposed compulsory enlistment for overseas service; my views in this regard have not altered. Allow me to quote an article published a few days ago, in one of our English Canadian newspapers:
Conscription is an ugly expression. It conveys the idea of compulsion and it is one of the worst words in the English language. It should be replaced by something nicer, perhaps general military training. This would sound better in the ears of a generation who prefers to keep fit rather than fat.

Could anyone state, in this house, that our war effort is not as complete as it should be, when one of our leaders has acknowledged that voluntary service has been more efficient than compulsory enlistment could ever have been; when, in our factories, we have everywhere exceeded the objectives set for our production? To mention but one case, I may state that, in the course of a visit by a number of members of parliament, on June 13, to the Canadian Car munitions plant at Saint Paul L'Ermite, we were informed that the weekly objective of 9,000 shells had been more than doubled and that, at the present time, that plant alone supplies, every week, more than
18,000	shells of all sizes. Have we not. done our share of the war effort when this house has unanimously consented to give Great Britain munitions and supplies to the amount of one billion dollars and when, furthermore, we are willing to lend the mother country $750,000,000 without interest for the duration? All this, Mr. Speaker, in a country whose population is less than 12 million inhabitants. What other British dominion has made such a tremendous war contribution in men, munitions, supplies and money? What other British dominion has adopted conscription for overseas service? On two separate occasions a bill of this nature has been rejected in Australia and neither India, New Zealand, South Africa, nor Northern Ireland have ever countenanced such a measure.
Until now, Quebec has done its full share in every field of endeavour. Have we forgotten that the very first regiment to be brought to full active force for overseas, service is a French-Canadian regiment, the Regiment de Maisonneuve?
Have we not subscribed generously and even oversubscribed our share of the war loans? Have not the workers in our plants, both men and women, produced beyond
expectation?
Let us face the facts squarely and ask ourselves if a change in the system would bring better results?
The Labour World reported the following quotation by E. M. Little, director of the national selective service, in its edition of May 23, 1942:
Every battle the united nations have lost in two and a half years was lost in the factory. Without exception there is the story from Norway to Bataan. When w'e Canadians get this seared into our minds as it has been in the minds of the defeated peoples of half a world, there will be no need for compulsion in organizing our man-power.
"Give us the tools," exclaimed Churchill, and we have responded generously in producing more than was expected of us. We supplied

Mobilization Act-Mr. Fuljord
the tools and the men. Is it not a fact that voluntary enlistments for overseas had reached in December last the substantial figure of
422.000	men, which must now be nearer the
500.000	mark.
We entered the war freely and we shall keep on doing our share.
In the last few days, conditions have changed and the war is getting nearer to us. The Japanese have already set foot on American territory. Let us then do nothing likely to divide Canada or to slow down our war effort.
Let us prepare to meet any attack by the enemy. Let us not forget Hong Kong, Singapore. Let us remember Australia, who when she was attacked had to send an S.O.S. to London but to no avail.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) unwittingly defined our policy when he stated, as reported at page 3291 of Hansard:
The decision on this question was taken out of my hands! It was made for me by an authority that I acknowledge to be my superior and to whom I owe a very willing obedience. It has been decided by the high court of the electors of the riding from which I come.
I take the same position. Having received an affirmative vote on the plebiscite, the hon. member considers himself bound to support the measure now before the house; my own electors having refused to relieve me of my past commitments, I must oppose any change in the Mobilization Act calling for compulsory enlistment for overseas service.
As the former minister of Public Works has said, should the proposed amendment be allowed to pass without debate or protest, it would be too late to protest later on. For this motive, Mr. Speaker, I regret my inability to accept the amendment to the Mobilization Act introduced in the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
It was at first with a bit of hesitation that I decided to enter this debate on what has become now the famous Bill No. 80. However, I feel that I would have been remiss in my duty had I not taken the opportunity to express to this house my views on the subject.
My very first recollections of the city of Ottawa are among my most treasured and prized memories, because as a child I remember being driven through a blinding snowstorm to the home of the late Sir Wilfrid and Lady Laurier. As I grew older I had the rare opportunity to repeat those visits, and it was through the influence of the great chieftain that I came to love my native land, my Canada, as I do. It was through the influence of- I was going to say the greatest-certainly one of the greatest of all Canadians that I came to know, to respect, to admire my French
compatriots, my fellow-Canadian citizens, to respect their traditions, to know their culture and something of their home life and their deep religious feeling. I therefore feel that I know my French compatriots a little better perhaps than d<# some other English members, and I hope that with that knowledge goes a large degree of understanding and tolerance.
(Translation) M. l'Orateur, je peux compren-dre cette belle langue, mais malheureusement je ne peux pas la parler parce que chez nous je n'ai pas 1'occasion.
(Text) It has always been a great source of pride to me as a Canadian to realize that this vast dominion of ours is composed of the two great races, the Anglo-Saxon and the French, each speaking his own language and each trying in a very difficult situation to keep this country united. Never was there a time when this need was more felt. I do not know of any monument quite like the one to Montcalm and Wolfe on the Plains of Abraham. To me it is the very essence of Canadian nationhood. It shows how two great races can and must and will live together in complete unity and harmony. True, we have had our differences. Unfortunately, we are having a difference right now; but have we ever known great friends who have not argued, who have not had their differences, and who afterwards have not become closer friends? I think that is an axiom of life.
In Europe the little country of Switzerland is even more complex in its make-up than are we. Although that country in size is hardly any larger than a good sized Ontario county, nevertheless there are four distinct sections in it. In one section Italian is spoken; just along the shores of lac Leman one finds French. By far the largest section of Switzerland speaks German, and one tiny little corner speaks what is known as Romanish, which is said by linguists to resemble ancient Latin more than any modern language. Yet Switzerland demonstrates the principles of true democracy better than any other European country even before the war? To-day it is the only democracy left on the European continent. Some may say that in Switzerland this is easy because the country is so small, but it is not so easy to keep it unified because of vast mountain ranges separating the various sections. For instance, to get from the French section along the shores of lac Leman one has to go through Simplon tunnel, under one of the highest spurs of the Alps. When one comes into the tunnel one hears only French spoken; when one emerges from the tunnel fifteen minutes later one hears only Italian. One sees a difference in the complexion of the people. Yet that seems to
Mobilization Act-Mr. Fuljord

make no difference. I think that when we have our little differences, as we do, we can well look to Switzerland as an example and remember that through thick and thin that little country has stayed a democracy; it has stayed unified and has defied all Europe- Napoleon, Hitler and the rest-to conquer it.
In 1937 I was privileged to visit the European continent. It was a rare opportunity because I doubt whether one will ever see Europe again as it was in those years. Certain aspects of European life I hope we shall never see again, but it is quite evident that the Europe that has survived for centuries, until 1939, will never be the same again. It is hard to visualize how peaceful the countries were through which we passed. Holland sat back quite confident that because of its complicated system of dykes and dams it could never be invaded by the Germans; that it might be bombed from the air but that it could never be invaded by the army. Well, Holland was one of the first European countries to fall. Brave little Belguim, which relied so much on its marvellously trained army and its system of superior fortifications, and on the Albert canal, did not last much longer after the Netherlands fell. And then France. Who would have thought that the valorous and courageous French, with their "liberte, egalite, fraternite", would have fallen under the heel of the German hordes? Yet France fell.
We see countries who are to-day fighting, presumably on the side of Germany, who are in reality no better off than the conquered nations. Take Austria. When I was in Austria in 1937 that country was in a period of frustration. They knew something was going to happen, though they did not know what. They dreaded Germany; they distrusted the Germans, and they were the very first to feel the effects of all the might of Hitler's monsters. Czechoslovakia was well aware of what was going to happen and was well prepared. Time and again they warned us what would happen, but the warnings went unheeded. The fortifications of Czechoslovakia were second to none in the world; they had built great armaments; and yet we allowed their warnings to go. There was nothing but complacency. Unless one has been in the fascist and nazi countries it is impossible to realize just what they are like. How would you like to be spat upon just because you were driving with a licence bearing the British sign-"G.B."? That is what happened to us. In Germany you dared not speak your mind; you felt you were constantly being watched; wherever you turned you saw the dreaded swastika. The country was at that time armed to the teeth.

You did not have to be a member of the intelligence branch of the British army or any other army to see what was going on; it was right before you-armies on the march, columns of mechanized forces travelling along the magnificent highways at fifty to sixty miles an hour, when the world was fooling itself saying that Germany could not use mechanized forces because they had artificial rubber and the tires would burn up if they travelled more than twenty-five miles an hour. I remember hearing that when I was in Great Britain. And Britain herself, brave Britain, hoping and thinking wishfully that this world conflict, this armageddon could be staved off.
I mention these facts because they all have a bearing on the present situation. Are we completely and entirely alive even to-day in Canada to the war situation? I had an opportunity of speaking with an intimate friend and close business associate from Shanghai who was on furlough in Canada last December and who, incidentally, arrived back in Shanghai just before the Japanese seized the city. He told me tales of the cruelty of the Japanese that would make one's blood run cold. One night for an hour he told of one atrocity after another until I had to tell him to stop; I could not stand it any more. It was cruelty beyond belief. All the things he said are substantiated in a series of articles now appearing in the Saturday Evening Post entitled, "I Escaped from Hong Kong" by Jan Henrik Marsman. It shows us in Canada what we are up against. Someone might say, "these are all places far away"; but what has happened in Europe, what is happening in Asia, can happen here. What does it mean? It means that if we, along with our allies, are not successful in defeating the forces of evil, we stand to lose our language, our religion, our freedom of thought, our courts of law, our rights of assembly, in fact everything we have come to consider nearest and dearest.
This brings me to the point where I feel that the government has to have the right to employ conscription. I agree with the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Durocher) that conscription is a nasty word, one of the most disagreeable in our language. Nevertheless we might as well call a spade a spade; this is a blitzkrieg, a lightning war; we do not know when or where the axis forces will strike next. Our government must have the right to conscript men for military service if and when the time arrives that reinforcements are necessary for those who have so valiantly and bravely offered their lives for their country.
One could not hear the sincere and impassioned remarks of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) without being touched. I do not think there was an

Mobilization Act-Mr. Fuljord
hon. member in this house who did not appreciate what it meant to that hon. gentleman to say what he did. But there were two or three things with which I could not agree. He spoke of the necessity of impressing upon the French Canadians the reasons for sending men to the battle-front. I could see the point of that up to the time of this war. But on the day Germany entered Poland, September 1, 1939, our thought had, of necessity, to change. This is not "England's war"- I use an old familiar phrase-this is humanity's war. This is not Canada's war; this is a war for survival of the democratic nations and of democratic principles in the world. We do not have to appeal to reason to know this; the facts are before us; we cannot miss them.
Then the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vereheres stated that for many years the province of Quebec had been told that conscription would never again be enforced. Those statements were made by all shades of political opinion in all sincerity. But was not the world told for an equal length of time that there would never be another war? The world lias had to change its opinion. It took Dunkirk really to arouse the United Kingdom. Then on top of Dunkirk came the frightful nights of blitzkrieg over the city of London and, in fact, all over the British isles, horrors of which none of us can know anything unless he has been through such a blitzkrieg. It took Pearl Harbour to awaken the United States. They are fully aware of the danger now, and they have a universal national selective draft in that country. In that connection, the one thing that Americans point the accusing finger at Canada about is the fact that they have conscription and we have not. They do not understand what a magnificent job this country has done, and they will not understand until this country is given the right to enforce conscription at such time as it is deemed necessary. Let us reverently pray that it will not take a Dunkirk or an air blitz over Ottawa or another Pearl Harbour to awaken Canada'. In addition, we have Hong Kong to remember and avenge. To-day Canada is not alone in this war, as far as north America is concerned; we have been joined by Mexico and the United States. We were first in this war, and we have to show them that in proportion we are going to do the best job. That is one thing for which Canadians are noted; when they start something they always finish it.
I do not intend to argue whether the plebiscite was right or wrong, but the fact remains that eight of the nine provinces voted "yes." In my own riding the "yes" vote was 86 per cent; in my own town of Brockville it 44561-213
was 89 per cent, and in Gananoque, the other urban municipality in the riding, it was 93 per cent. I know whereof I speak when I say that by far the great majority of the people in the riding who voted "yes" did so with the thought that they were voting for some sort of conscription. The exact wording of the question on the ballot paper was:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
I grant you, sir, that there was nothing in that to make one believe he was voting either for or against conscription; but the fact remains that no matter what my revered leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or his ministers or I had to say, the feeling was that when the voters marked an X opposite "yes" they were voting for conscription. At this point I should like to give credit to two organizations that were of the greatest help in getting out the vote-the Canadian Legion and certain labour unions in the town in which I live. The Canadian Legion made a point of attending all the meetings held throughout the riding; they organized car drivers, provided speakers at meetings, and saw that the largest possible number of voters got out. That may serve to indicate how the people conceived the idea that they were voting on conscription, because everyone in Canada knows how the legion feels on the subject of national selective service. Personally I am in favour of conscription, in spite of the fact that it proved to be a failure in the last war. I consider it to be by far the fairest, most equitable and surest way of raising an army or of obtaining reinforcements. On February 3, 1942, when I was speaking in this house I mentioned a telephone call that I had received from one of the members of the committee of two hundred; and these words, which appear at page 272 of Hansard, I think set forth my position very clearly:
Some weeks ago I was telephoned by a member of the committee of two hundred which was meeting in Toronto with the alleged object of advancing Canada's war effort. I was asked if I favoured the policies advocated by this committee. I said in reply that if what they were after was national selective service with complete mobilization of all our man-power and resources, I was heartily behind them, but that if it was only conscription of men for overseas service, I was diametrically opposed to that.

Then I can serve the same purpose by saying that I have stated previously that I am unequivocally in favour of conscription of man-power along with conscription of resources. Nearly half a million young Canadians have decided that the best way to keep this war from our shores is to fight our enemies abroad, three thousand miles away. Their deeds, when recorded in history, will make every Canadian proud of the country of his birth. We cannot let these young men down. They must have adequate reinforcements. Fortunately, up to date our army casualties have been very light, simply because our men have not been in the fore-front of battle. The day will come, however, when the continent of Europe will be invaded. Then reinforcements will be needed, and then, after Bill No. 80 is passed, the government will have to decide whether it is necessary to raise men for reinforcements by conscription. I must congratulate the Prime Minister upon the method he has devised to meet the situation. We are actually debating conscription now; but if the time should come when it is found necessary to enforce conscription, then it can be applied by order in council, thereby relieving this house and the country of the pain of having old wounds reopened and new hard feelings created.
I have no alternative; I must follow the dictates of my conscience. I must support Bill No. 80 and, sir, I urge all to do likewise. I urge this for the sake of Canada, for the sake of the empire, for the sake of civilization and humanity.
On motion of Mr. Howe the debate was adjourned.
